newsitem.title: UK: Experts find out why salty taste appeals.
newsitem.headline: Experts find out why salty taste appeals.

text.p: Salt may taste so good in food because it masks bitter flavours and enhances sweet ones, U.S. food researchers said on Wednesday.
Paul Breslin and Gary Beauchamp of the Monell Chemical Senses Centre in Philadelphia said experiments they had done showed that salt acted as a kind of flavour filter.
Their tests on 21 volunteers cleared up the puzzling results found in other studies that have found that salt had little effect on other flavours.

"We used mixtures of aqueous solutions of a bitter substance, urea, which is strongly suppressed by sodium compounds; a sweetener, sucrose; and a salt, sodium acetate, which has a fairly mild taste," they wrote in a letter to the science journal Nature.
The volunteers were asked to rate how salty, sweet or bitter the drinks were.

"As predicted, there was a selective suppression of the taste components by sodium acetate," they wrote. "The bitterness of urea was suppressed much more by the salt than was the sweetness of sucrose."
When all three chemicals were put into the water, the mixture was sweeter than if the salt was not in there, they added.

"Our data show that, in addition to adding desired saltiness to food, salts potentiate flavour through the selective suppression of bitterness (and perhaps other undesirable flavours), and the release from suppression of palatable flavours such as sweetness," they said.

"The desire for sodium chloride (table salt) and other salts in foods as diverse as (often bitter) vegetables, oily foods and meats may be due in part to their ability to suppress unpleasant flavours."
This could be why low-sodium foods did not sell well. Perhaps efforts to market good low-salt substitutes should focus on blocking bitter taste, Breslin and Beauchamp suggested.
